public_rationale: The verified survey documents recurring cleanup and consequential low-quality output among workplace AI users. This supports often in the ordinary sense of a common practical problem. It does not show that most outputs are workslop or that AI usually reduces productivity. The same research reports widespread benefits, and the result depends on reading the claim as recurring workplace experience rather than a precise output failure rate.
limitations: Self-reported experience is not an independently graded output sample.
The surveyed population does not represent every occupation, country or model.
Survey sponsorship and unweighted sampling limit generalization.
The selected observation period precedes the post because the claim supplies no period and current usage cannot be reconstructed from publication dates.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Large language models often produce low-quality 'workslop'.

statement.document_title: Turns out Generative AI was a scam

our_interpretation: They refers to large language models.
Workslop means superficially useful workplace output that lacks accuracy, substance or necessary context and creates correction work.
Read often as a recurring practical problem encountered by many users, rather than a claim that most generated outputs are poor.
Use the latest clearly dated relevant fieldwork verified in readable sources available before the post: the November 13–14, 2025 enterprise-user survey. Older studies provide context.
Worker surveys can establish recurring experiences but cannot directly measure the fraction of all LLM outputs that are workslop.
criteria.support_condition: Credible workplace evidence shows that low-quality AI output and consequential correction work recur for a substantial share of users.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Broad, methodologically credible workplace evidence shows that such output and consequential correction work are rare under ordinary use.

evidence.excerpt: Only 2% say they generally don’t need to revise what AI produces.
evidence.locator: Key Survey Findings; About the Survey
evidence.explanation: The survey of 1,100 US AI users at larger employers also reports weekly cleanup and negative consequences from low-quality outputs. Together these support recurring workslop, although revision alone does not necessarily indicate poor quality.

evidence.excerpt: Just 69% say AI helps, compared to 94% of trained workers.
evidence.explanation: Reported benefits remain common even alongside cleanup, and training is associated with different experiences. This limits any inference that recurring workslop makes AI generally unhelpful.

evidence.excerpt: Two-thirds of workers report spending up to six or more hours each week correcting AI-related errors.
evidence.locator: The Hidden Cost to Workers; Methodology
evidence.explanation: This release describes recurring correction work among respondents already screened for encountering workslop. Its methodology explicitly dates fieldwork to January 8, 2025, so it is neither current-period evidence nor an estimate of prevalence among all workers.
